lesson.title: Building the Support You Later Take Away
lesson.summary: Scaffolding is the temporary, adjustable support a more skilled person gives a learner within their zone of proximal development, gradually withdrawn as the learner gains independence.
lesson.body:
Scaffolding is the practical technique that puts the zone of proximal development to work. It refers to the temporary support a teacher, parent, or more skilled peer provides to help a learner accomplish a task that sits within their zone of proximal development, support that is deliberately structured to be reduced and eventually removed as the learner becomes able to do the task alone. The term itself was introduced later by researchers building on Vygotsky's ideas, not by Vygotsky himself, but it captures exactly what his theory implies about good teaching: help should target the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with assistance, not tasks they have already mastered or tasks that remain impossible even with help.

The metaphor is doing real work here. Construction scaffolding is put up around a building while it is being worked on, and it is taken down once the structure can stand on its own. Good instructional scaffolding behaves the same way. A parent teaching a child to tie shoes might first tie the laces together for them, then physically guide their hands through the motions, then talk them through each step verbally while the child's hands do the work, then just watch and offer a reminder only when needed, and finally step back entirely. At each stage the amount and kind of support shrinks as the child's own competence grows, always staying just ahead of what the child can already do alone.

Effective scaffolding has a few recognizable features: it is calibrated to the individual learner's current zone of proximal development rather than a one-size-fits-all script, it is temporary by design rather than a permanent crutch, and it is responsive, meaning the helper is constantly reading how much the learner needs and adjusting in real time. Too much scaffolding, help that persists after a learner could manage alone, can slow the development of independence. Too little, pushing a learner to attempt tasks well outside their zone of proximal development with no support, tends to produce frustration rather than learning. The goal is always the same: use guided interaction to help a learner do today, with help, what they will be able to do tomorrow, alone.
